top_comments: People like to get sanctimonious about blocking ads, but this is one of the many good reasons why I'll never feel bad about it.

Worth noting that this isn’t really anything to do with the technical capabilities of WebRTC, it’s just that it’s less frequently monitored for nefarious behavior. Same reason they’re only targeting mobile devices: harder to detect.No reason this approach couldn’t be taken with simple HTTP requests. If you’re embedding third party scripts on your site you’re always vulnerable.

One basic design no-go of the www is to allow strangers to run random code on your computer. It is just not acceptable. Servers should deliver just data and my browser decides what to do with it. A shop should deliver lists of items and prizes and my shop browser decides how to operate with the catalogue in a way I want. Everying else is nuts.

articles.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
articles.summary: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.I made this game! Some technical details:The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

top_comments: Fun little game, but the drop needs to be slower so it is easier to bet. Odds jumping from 0.01 to 0.99 in like one tenth of a second makes it hard to play
Completely ignoring the ball and just buying cheap shares is a surprisingly efficient strategy. Often I'm able to get both kinds of share for cheap, so I win regardless of the outcome.

It is true soundness bugs have been found, and the Lean community spends effort on it. But this page doesn't convey the gap between one incorrect verification and successfully misleading mathematicians about what is true: there are multiple checkers and you need bugs in all of them, without the input looking implausible on informal review.(For example, a DeepMind researcher created a 'proof' that passed Lean and (a then-week-old version of) nanoda by exploiting a different bug in each. But if you fed that into a regular old LLM (or to a human expert, but I mention LLMs b/c they can be assigned to review even very large volumes of Lean code) it would immediately say "no, this isn't real math.")The increase in soundness bugs found this year is notable, because LLMs are good at finding ways to their assigned goals, and they found some funny ones. And, besides fixes for the specific bugs, it led to broader work on hardening and alternative and verified kernels: https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-...So you have fewer avenues than at the start of the year to get a proof of False OK'd by one proof-checker kernel, and it's much much harder to get one through the gauntlet invoked by `lake check --paranoid`.(This is also interesting as a(nother) example of the difficulty of making truly correct software -- you'd hope for proof-checker kernels to be pretty high on the correctness scale but seems like we've found 16-32 soundness bugs in a bunch of these.)

I think this is misleading for the proof-checkers in systems where multiple provers must pass for the proof to be accepted.In the case of Metamath, yes, soundness bugs have been found in the original "metamath" proof verifier, written in C. But to be accepted into the main proof databases (set.mm and iset.mm), proofs must pass "5 independently-created verifiers in 5 different programming languages: metamath (a C verifier by Norm Megill), mmj2 (a Java verifier by Mel O'Cat and Mario Carneiro), smetamath-rs (a high-speed Rust verifier by Stefan O'Rear), checkmm (a C++ verifier by Eric Schmidt), and mmverify.py a Python verifier by Raph Levien)." - https://us.metamath.org/To me, that's a key countermeasure to the problem.

The call for further high-assurance work is good, but let's not miss the forest for the trees: some of these have been around for decades, and all the soundness bugs they've ever had fit in a tweet! (Or close to it.)Comfortably more than good enough for 99.9% of software, especially considering you'd still need to exploit such a soundness bug in a way that hides a further issue in the program being verified.

articles.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
articles.summary: Hi HN!I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges thereI'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance

top_comments: > It can only move in ways the maths allows.This property is desirable for a tool that assists you in performing work, but actually undesirable for a tool designed to guide your learning: it means you are protected from doing something wrong (much like when they put up the bumpers/siderails at a bowling alley), the result being that you receive no feedback when your mental model requires adjustment.

"Declarative Dragging" co-author here. It's wonderful to see our work encouraging you to explore this space of interaction. Thanks for sharing!You might be interested in checking out:- Graspable Math: https://activities.graspablemath.com/- our (cursorily vibe-coded) demo based on Graspable Math: https://declarative-dragging.github.io/dragology/#/demos/gra...
